clinical_category: Calcium supplementation - dose splitting and absorption
blueprint_topic: Safe supplement administration and client education
stem: A client has been instructed to take 1,000 mg/day of supplemental elemental calcium and plans to take the entire amount as calcium carbonate at one time. Which teaching by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Split the supplemental calcium into doses of 500 mg or less and take calcium carbonate with food because absorption decreases as the amount taken at one time increases.
options.B: Take the full 1,000 mg at one time on an empty stomach because larger single doses of calcium carbonate are absorbed more completely.
options.C: Take calcium carbonate only at bedtime without food because meals prevent absorption of this form of calcium.
options.D: The size and timing of each calcium dose do not affect absorption, so there is no reason to divide the supplement.

rationale: A is correct. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements states that calcium absorption from supplements is highest with doses of 500 mg or less at one time and that the percentage absorbed decreases as the amount of elemental calcium taken at once increases. Calcium carbonate is absorbed best when taken with food because its absorption depends more on gastric acid; calcium citrate is less dependent on gastric acid and can be taken with or without food. B, C, and D contradict these absorption principles. The stem specifies that the client's clinician has already directed 1,000 mg/day of supplemental calcium; the item therefore tests administration of that existing plan rather than independently recommending a daily calcium requirement.
educational_objective: Optimize calcium-supplement absorption by dividing supplemental elemental calcium into doses of 500 mg or less and taking calcium carbonate with food while distinguishing it from calcium citrate.
source_organization: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Office of Dietary Supplements
source_document_title: Calcium — Health Professional Fact Sheet; Calcium — Consumer Fact Sheet
source_version_date: Current NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NIH ODS 'Calcium — Health Professional Fact Sheet' → Sources of Calcium → Dietary supplements: absorption from supplements is highest with doses of 500 mg or less; percentage absorbed decreases as the amount taken at one time rises; calcium carbonate absorption is better with a meal and calcium citrate is less dependent on stomach acid. NIH ODS 'Calcium — Consumer' → 'What kinds of calcium dietary supplements are available?': calcium carbonate is absorbed best with food; calcium citrate can be taken with or without food; if taking 1,000 mg/day from supplements, smaller divided doses are preferable to a single dose.
source_claim_supported: Current NIH ODS sources directly support the 500-mg-or-less per-dose absorption guidance, divided dosing, and the food-dependent absorption difference between calcium carbonate and calcium citrate.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 12 (PDF pageno 15): review medication-related data, educate clients about medications and evaluate safe administration practices.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's vague divided-dose teaching into a precise administration scenario using NIH ODS rather than a generic osteoporosis-foundation citation. The final item directly supports the ≤500 mg per-dose threshold and specifies calcium carbonate so the food instruction is unambiguous. The 1,000 mg/day amount is presented as an existing clinician-directed regimen, not as a universal daily recommendation.
audit_findings: The source core concept was correct but relied on a generic secondary source and lacked an exact evidence-backed dose threshold.
Fresh NIH ODS review directly verifies that supplement absorption is highest at 500 mg or less per dose and decreases with larger single doses.
The final item specifies calcium carbonate so the food instruction is directly supported and does not create ambiguity with calcium citrate.
Distractors test large-dose/empty-stomach use, bedtime fasting and denial of dose-size effects; none is defensible.
